source.title: scGPT: Towards Building a Foundation Model for Single-Cell Multi-omics Using Generative AI
source.authors: Haotian Cui; Chloe Wang; H. Maan; Kuan Pang; Fengning Luo; Bo Wang

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling analysis to generative pretraining on single-cell biological data, assessing how pretraining-data size relates to embeddings and downstream performance. It does not reproduce language-model held-out-loss or compute-optimal-allocation measurements.
record.gate_note: The authors cite Kaplan et al. and report their own pretraining-data-size comparisons. The reported outcomes are cell-embedding quality and downstream-task performance, not held-out cross-entropy loss; they do not fit parameter-, token- or compute-scaling power laws or test compute-optimal allocations. Results from unrelated task benchmarks are not included.
record.test_reason: The study pretrains scGPT, a single-cell transformer, on 30K, 300K, 3M and 33M cells at fixed parameter count. It then reports fine-tuned cell-type annotation accuracy across these sizes. This bears on whether downstream performance improves with pretraining scale in a non-text modality. No held-out loss is reported and no power law is fitted, so only a monotonic-trend form of V6 is tested here. V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors claim to 'confirm the scaling law': larger pretraining data gives better embeddings and downstream performance. They note apparent saturation after 3M cells and only hypothesise that larger models would lift it; model size is not tested. They also find that pretraining-context relevance matters at fixed data size.
record.recipe_differences: This is a single-cell biological foundation-model study. It varies pretraining cell count at fixed parameter count and evaluates embeddings or downstream performance, rather than fitting language-model held-out-loss scaling laws or testing compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Pretraining data context changes downstream integration performance; the brain-pretrained model trailed the blood-pretrained model by 8% despite similar dataset size. The authors also note possible saturation of the data-size trend after 3M cells.

fits_no_version.finding: At similar pretraining size (~13M cells), a brain-pretrained model trailed a blood-pretrained model by 8% AvgBIO on COVID-19 integration. Data relevance, not size alone, drives downstream gains.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream gains from pretraining scale depend on domain relevance of the pretraining data.

fits_no_version.finding: Organ-specific models trained on >800K cells gave visibly better cell-type separation in UMAP embeddings. This is qualitative and confounded with organ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Embedding quality improves above a pretraining-data threshold in single-cell models.

record.problems: The size-scaling results are described qualitatively in the text while plotted accuracy values are not available in the supplied text. No power-law fit or extrapolation is reported, and the paper notes possible saturation after 3M cells. The downstream context comparison indicates a substantial context effect.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss, no parameter or compute sweep, no power-law fit.
No shape comparison at fixed parameters.
The power-law form in single-cell data is not assessed. Only downstream accuracy is measured, with no held-out loss and no fit.
The trend is shown on one task (MS annotation) only. There is no predictive fit, no relation to pretraining loss, and no model-size scaling.

missing.what: MS annotation accuracy for the 33M model is 0.856, versus 0.798 for the from-scratch model (no pretraining). This gives a numeric endpoint and a zero-data baseline for the scaling series.

record.verdict_notes: The 'scaling law' here is the authors' label for a monotonic trend in downstream accuracy over four data sizes. No loss, power-law fit or exponent is reported. Single-cell data counts as a new modality, but V5's power-law form is untested. The saturation after 3M at fixed parameters is consistent with V1's bottleneck caveat rather than contradicting it.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss, parameter/token/compute scaling sweep, or power-law loss fit.
No small-run power-law extrapolation or comparison of such predictions with larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or estimate of optimal parameter and token counts.
No comparison of architecture depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.

The study examines single-cell biological pretraining data size and embedding quality, but does not fit or verify a power-law form, measure held-out cross-entropy, or test other modalities and regimes such as image/video, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.

Tests pretraining-data size for cell-type annotation and reports context effects for COVID-19 integration; does not establish a predictive curve across multiple downstream tasks or relate performance to pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents or fitting choices, and no analysis of curves bending away from a power law.

rows.subject: scGPT organ-specific models
rows.size_stated: Models trained on more than 800,000 cells are distinguished from those trained on fewer cells; individual model sizes are not stated here.
rows.operation_detail: Compared cell embeddings from organ-specific models trained on different amounts of data.

conditions.value: More than 800,000 cells versus less than or equal to 800,000 cells

rows.value: Models trained on more than 800,000 cells were reported to generate embeddings that better separated cell types.
rows.note: This is a qualitative threshold-based result, not a fitted power law. The text summarizes the organ-specific models collectively.
rows.check: This is a qualitative UMAP threshold judgement (>800K cells) across organ-specific models. Data size is confounded with organ, and the measure is embedding separation, not loss or task performance. It is not a scaling measurement of any version.

rows.subject: scGPT brain-pretrained model
rows.stage_stated: Pre-trained on brain cells, then fine-tuned for integration.
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream COVID-19 dataset integration performance across models pretrained on different cellular contexts.
rows.baseline: Blood-pretrained model with a similar dataset size
rows.uncertainty: Standard error across five integration experiments is described for Figure S8; the value for this comparison is not stated.
rows.locator: Section 2.6; Supplementary Note S.1 and Figure S8
rows.note: The authors attribute the difference to relevance of cellular context, showing downstream performance is not determined by pretraining data size alone.
rows.check: This compares pretraining context (brain vs blood) at similar data size. It is not a scale manipulation, so it does not bear on any version's scaling claim. It belongs in fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: scGPT at fixed parameter count, MS cell-type annotation, pretraining 30K→3M cells
relationships.reason: Fine-tuned annotation accuracy rises as pretraining cells grow (r1-r3, Fig 2F). Values are figure-only and no predictive fit is given.
relationships.display_finding: Fine-tuned annotation accuracy increased as pretraining expanded from 30K to 3M cells, without a predictive fit.

relationships.reason: The authors note apparent saturation after 3M cells and attribute it to the fixed model size; this is untested (r4).
relationships.display_finding: Performance appeared to saturate after 3M cells, which the authors attributed to fixed model size without testing that explanation.
